newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl says Bonn united in drive for euro.
newsitem.headline: Kohl says Bonn united in drive for euro.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl, fending off increasingly shrill attacks from a hardline conservative rival, said on Monday his government was fully united in its drive to launch the single European Union currency on time in 1999.

Brushing off doubts about the euro raised by Bavarian premier Edmund Stoiber, Kohl said he was certain economic and monetary union (EMU) would be launched without delay. He said his government was completely committed to the project.

"We are steering a clear course for introducing the euro (currency) without any ifs or buts," Kohl said at a news conference held in Berlin after a meeting of leaders from his Christian Democratic Union (CDU).

Stoiber, a leader of the CDU's Bavarian sister party the Christian Social Union (CSU), has annoyed Kohl with his near-daily criticism of the euro. In a thinly veiled broadside at Stoiber, Kohl said Germany would meet the tough fiscal criteria spelled out in the EU's Maastricht Treaty.

"The entry criterion of 3.0 percent (of gross domestic product) will not be watered down," Kohl said, offering journalists an answer to Stoiber's charges that the euro should be delayed if Germany fails to meet that target.
Asked about the criticism from Stoiber, Kohl said: "I do not want to comment on that. Stoiber should speak for himself."

Kohl was not originally due to speak to journalists. But, apparently annoyed over Stoiber's non-stop potshots at the euro, he decided he would address the news conference, taking over for CDU general secretary Peter Hintze.
Kohl and Stoiber will both be speaking at the same event in Munich on Tuesday, but have no plans to meet each other.

The chancellor, one of the architects of the single European currency and certainly one of its most ardent backers, has widespread support for his position in his centre-right coalition even if public opinion polls side with Stoiber.
The Free Democrats (FDP), junior partners in Kohl's coalition, warned the debate stoked by Stoiber could cause irreparable harm to the centre-right coalition.
Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt and other FDP leaders decried the persistent hardline warnings against any relaxation of the criteria for the euro from Stoiber.
German editorial writers also took aim at Stoiber, whose indefatigable warnings about meeting strict fiscal criteria for EMU have drawn strong rebukes from Kohl and the CDU.
Stoiber has opposed CDU leaders, insisting on strict interpretation of the Maastricht Treaty outlining economic criteria for EMU.

"This could cause damage to the coalition in the long run," said Guido Westerwelle, general secretary of the FDP. "Stoiber is not interested in the stability of the euro. He is more interested in his chances for the next Bavarian elections."
Rexrodt warned the debate could damage business.

"From the view of the German economy, a renewed delay debate is dangerous," Rexrodt said. "The German business sector must be able to rely on the start date to be able to make the necessary preparations for the currency change-over on time."
Oskar Lafontaine, leader of the opposition Social Democrats (SPD), derided the hardline insistence of holding the budget deficit to three percent of GDP.
"This fetish for 3.0 is economic nonsense," he said. "If the project failed, it would be a setback for European unity."
Many German newspaper editorial writers said Stoiber's anti-euro campaign had little to do with the single currency.
The populist premier's stance had more to do with raising his own personal political profile and showing his CSU party standing up to Kohl in Bonn ahead of state elections next year.
The Frankfurter Rundschau newspaper said Stoiber was likely to stick to his stance. "He won't simply knuckle under just because Helmut Kohl wrinkles his brow in annoyance," it said.
The liberal daily warned of danger for Kohl if he decided to be less than rigid in applying deficit criteria rules.
"Stoiber would mobilise the CSU against this and presumably, find a clear majority in favour of his stance," it predicted. "That would mean the end of the coalition in Bonn."
